title: Chapter XVI
focus: rejection and the turn to revenge

teacherSummary.text: The De Laceys abandon the cottage. Enraged, the creature burns it and heads for Geneva, guided by Victor's journal. He saves a drowning girl but is shot. Near Geneva he meets William, learns he is a Frankenstein, kills him, and plants the portrait on the sleeping Justine.

vocabulary.definition: To call down by prayer, as something hurtful or calamitous
vocabulary.context: Oh, earth! how often did I imprecate curses on the cause of my being!
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “imprecate”: im- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To moisten with dew, or as with dew
vocabulary.context: Soft tears again bedewed my cheeks, and I even raised my humid eyes with thankfulness towards the blessed sun which bestowed such joy upon me.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “bedew”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Small trees and bushes that grow among large trees
vocabulary.context: Accordingly I hid myself in some thick underwood, determining to devote the ensuing hours to reflection on my situation.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “underwood”: un- (Old English un-, "not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Thanks to the lessons of Felix and the sanguinary laws of man, I had learned now to work mischief.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “sanguinary”: -ary (Latin -arius, "connected with"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: The ball had entered my shoulder, and I knew not whether it had remained there or passed through; at any rate I had no means of extracting it.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “extract”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of") + tract (Latin trahere, "to draw, pull"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: An adjective expressing some quality, attribute, or relation, that is properly or specially appropriate to a person…
vocabulary.context: “The child still struggled, and loaded me with epithets which carried despair to my heart; I grasped his throat to silence him, and in a moment he lay dead at my feet.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “epithet”: the (Greek theos, "god"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: I was like a wild beast that had broken the toils; destroying the objects that obstructed me, and ranging through the wood with a stag-like swiftness.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “obstruct”: ob- (Latin ob, "against, toward") + struct (Latin struere, "to build"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: I trembled violently, apprehending some dreadful misfortune.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “apprehend”: ap- (Latin ad, "to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: The nearer I approached to your habitation, the more deeply did I feel the spirit of revenge enkindled in my heart.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “enkindle”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To bestow a share or portion of
vocabulary.context: Here, I thought, is one of those whose joy-imparting smiles are bestowed on all but me.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “impart”: im- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: This chapter retells Chapter VII's events from the other side—a key structural mirror.

significance: His turn to violence complicates sympathy: rejection explains but does not excuse his crimes.
discussionQuestions: Does the creature's suffering excuse what he does to William and Justine?
Where does irony appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with creation and responsibility?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XVI,” how does Shelley show rejection and the turn to revenge? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XVI, how does Shelley develop the idea of rejection and the turn to revenge? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the irony in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XVI develops the idea of rejection and the turn to revenge. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XVI (where it begins, turns and ends) and its irony shape the reader's understanding of rejection and the turn to revenge. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XVI suggests about rejection and the turn to revenge. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's irony and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses irony in Chapter XVI to complicate the reader's understanding of rejection and the turn to revenge. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XVI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of rejection and the turn to revenge responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XVI alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of rejection and the turn to revenge follows or bends those conventions, using the irony as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XVI and its treatment of rejection and the turn to revenge. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's irony and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XVI as evidence for a larger claim about rejection and the turn to revenge in Frankenstein. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XVI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of rejection and the turn to revenge. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

satQuestions.passage: “When night came, I quitted my retreat, and wandered in the wood; and now, no longer restrained by the fear of discovery, I gave vent to my anguish in fearful howlings. I was like a wild beast that had broken the toils; destroying the objects that obstructed me, and ranging through the wood with a stag-like swiftness. O! what a miserable night I passed! the cold stars shone in mockery, and the bare trees waved their branches above me: now and then the sweet voice of a bird burst forth amidst the universal stillness. All, save I, were at rest or in enjoyment: I, like the archfiend, bore a hell within me; and, finding myself unsympathised with, wished to tear up the trees, spread havoc and destruction around me, and then to have sat down and enjoyed the ruin.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XVI”?
options: Rejection and the turn to revenge

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Does the creature's suffering excuse what he does to William and Justine? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are imprecate, bedewed, underwood, sanguinary, extracting. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Oh, earth! how often did I imprecate curses on the cause of my being!” Webster's says: To call down by prayer, as something hurtful or calamitous. Now the word history: “imprecate”: im- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “bedew”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “underwood”: un- (Old English un-, "not"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. This chapter retells Chapter VII's events from the other side—a key structural mirror. Why does this chapter matter? His turn to violence complicates sympathy: rejection explains but does not excuse his crimes. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for irony.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see irony, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to rejection and the turn to revenge.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Irony, Characterization, Foreshadowing.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of irony. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XVI,” how does Shelley show rejection and the turn to revenge? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about rejection and the turn to revenge, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
